title: Student Loan Shake-Up: July 1 Brings New Repayment Plans and Borrowing Caps
summary: A seismic shift in student loan policy arrives July 1, as provisions from last year's One Big Beautiful Bill Act take effect. The changes end the Biden-era SAVE plan, introduce two Republican-designed repayment options, and impose strict new borrowing limits for graduate students. For the more than 7 million borrowers currently enrolled in SAVE—the most generous income-driven repayment plan—the clock is ticking. The Department of Education will send notices giving roughly 90 days to choose a new plan. If you don't act, you'll be automatically placed in one of the least flexible options. Financial aid experts warn this could worsen an alarming rise in defaults, since many SAVE enrollees qualified for $0 monthly payments due to low incomes. Borrowers with existing loans who aren't planning to borrow more will have several repayment choices, including the brand-new Repayment Assistance Plan (RAP) and Tiered Standard Plan. The department's Loan Simulator can help compare options. But if you take out any new loan on or after July 1, your choices narrow to just those two new plans. Graduate students face the most dramatic changes. Previously, they could borrow up to the full cost of their program. Starting July 1, the cap drops to $20,500 per year and $100,000 total. A small group of professional degrees—including medicine, law, and dentistry—qualify for higher limits of $50,000 annually and $200,000 aggregate. Advocates fear these caps could lead to shortages in nursing and other healthcare fields. Undergraduate borrowing limits remain unchanged: dependent students can borrow up to $31,000 total, independent students up to $57,500. The Education Department is making some exceptions for grad students already mid-program. As the landscape shifts, borrowers should review their status now to avoid costly surprises.
why_it_matters: This story shows how government decisions directly affect young people's futures. Understanding how student loans work now can help you make smarter choices about college and avoid being trapped by debt later.

background_read: Over the past decade, the U.S. has seen intense debate over student loan debt, which now exceeds $1.7 trillion. Income-driven repayment plans, introduced in 2009, let borrowers pay a percentage of their income instead of a fixed amount. The SAVE plan (Saving on a Valuable Education), launched by the Biden administration, was the most generous—offering $0 monthly payments to those with very low incomes and forgiving remaining balances after a set number of years. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, a major Republican budget measure passed in 2024, reversed many of those policies and imposed new borrowing caps. The Department of Education, the federal agency overseeing student aid and the implementation of these rules, must now enforce the changes. Historically, tightening borrowing limits has aimed to reduce government spending, but it also raises concerns about access to advanced degrees and fields like nursing.

perspectives.description: Supporters argue the changes will save taxpayers billions and encourage students to choose shorter, job-ready degrees instead of taking on endless debt. By capping graduate loans, the government hopes to prevent overborrowing for programs that don't lead to high incomes. This could shift focus toward more affordable education paths and reduce the burden on federal budgets.

Critics say ending SAVE and capping loans will punish low-income and middle-class students who can only afford higher education with generous repayment options. The automatic placement into less flexible plans could push millions into delinquency or default. Fields like nursing, which already face shortages, may lose talent because students can't afford graduate training without borrowing beyond the new limits.

Student loan policy has seesawed between administrations for years. The original SAVE plan was a Democratic priority; its repeal reflects the current Republican majority's belief in limited government aid. From a systemic view, such rapid rule changes make long-term planning difficult for families and colleges, creating a cycle of boom-and-bust in enrollment and lending.

Future administrations could reinstate more generous plans, but for now students and families must navigate a much tougher borrowing landscape. This could accelerate the shift toward online education, community colleges, and employer-funded degrees. Over time, if workforce shortages emerge in essential fields, Congress might be pressured to carve out more professional exemptions or rethink the caps.
